subject: Patch adding matrix/vector scalar subtraction (plus bug fix)

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Patch adding matrix/vector scalar subtraction (plus bug fix)
parts:
So I implemented subtraction by a scalar in stan.  I've attached a patch.  I tried to follow convention as best as I could determine, hopefully I got close.  If everything is ok, I'll finish and add scalar addition.  (I started with subtraction because it was what was immediately necessary for my model.  In retrospect, addition would have been more generally useful.  Ah well.)

Also included in the patch is a very small fix to the element-wise division that was recently added.  One function was named elt_division when (I assume) it was meant to be elt_divide.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Patch adding matrix/vector scalar subtraction (plus bug fix)
parts:
One question for EVERYONE (marked below as such), and
one for BEN (ditto).

On 3/7/12 3:26 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> So I implemented subtraction by a scalar in stan. I've attached a
> patch.

Thanks for the code and heads up about the misnamed
divide operator. Yes, it's very close to the conventions
we've used.

We can add you (Marcus) as a committer to the Stan project
so this doesn't all have to go through e-mails. How do
you feel about doc and unit tests? You can find the tests
under stan/test -- we're using the googletest framework, which
is like JUnit for Java.


?? for EVERYONE:
-----------------
As to this specific patch (and presumably its sibling,
addition by scalar), what does everyone else think about
having this kind of broadcasting of constants up to
appropriately sized vectors or matrices? With v a vector,
m a matrix, and c a scalar, this would be:

vector: (v - c)(i) = v(i) - c

matrix: (m - c)(i,j) = m(i,j) - c

Is this something that's done in MATLAB? In standard
vector notation?


I also have some (long) comments on efficiency and some of
the standards we've tried to follow. Your implementation (for
matrices) is:

inline matrix_d subtract(const matrix_d& m, const double& c) {
matrix_d c_(m.rows(),m.cols());
c_.fill(c);
return m - c_;
}

I'm wondering if it'd be more efficient to do this explicitly:

inline matrix_d subtract(const matrix_d& m, const double c) {
matrix_d mc(m.rows(),m.cols());
for (int i = 0; i < c.size(); ++i)
mc(i) = m(i) - c;
return mc;
}

This unfortunately relies on fixed row-major or column-major
ordering because it uses unary accessors.

But then your last line, "return m - c_;" should be using
a template expression for (m - c_) rather than allocating, so
the return-by-value should copy directly without creating
an intermediate in situations like:

matrix_d mc = m - c;

So they're probably very similar in terms of performance, with
the only difference being the second loop through the data
done by fill(c).


?? for BEN:
-----------
What we'd really like is a no-allocation template expression
for a constant M x N matrix (like your "c_"), but I can't figure
out how to do that in Eigen (CwiseNullaryOp, as returned
by Constant() looks promising). Ben?


You can use size() on matrices and it gives you rows * cols.
This is potentially unsafe if m doesn't have the default
row-major/col-major setting. We've just stuck with the col-major
defaults, so it'll be OK as called from Stan, but not as a general
API function. A full double loop is safer, but much less efficient
in that there's all the index arithmetic

for (int j = 0; j < c.cols(); ++j)
for (int i = 0; i < c.rows(); ++i)
mc(i,j) = m(i,j) - c

We stuck with Eigen's col-major default, so
the loop should at least be col-major.

We relaly want that constant template expression.

We've saved the "x_" style of variables for class member variables
to separate them visually from local variables (we've also been
inconsistent and used "_x" and I used "x__" inside of models to
avoid name clashes with Stan variables).

I haven't profiled, but every piece of advice I've ever
seen says that doubles should be passed by value where
possible. There are some clever ways to template out an arg
so that it's by value for primitives and otherwise by ref --
Alexandrescu discusses this in his C++ book and the approach
is implemented more or less in Boost. But we haven't gone that
far down the optimization path, yet. I'd rather get things
working before getting too carried away on optimization (despite
how I may sound in this e-mail).

We don't want to promote a matrix or vector of scalars to
an auto dif variable (using to_var()) unless we have to,
as the creation of auto-dif variables is expensive.
I plan to go back in and optimize all the vector ops to
avoid many of the to_var() that are there and also partially
evaluate the auto-difs as we've already done for the basic
functions.

The code's essentially the same:

template <typename T1, typename T2>
inline Matrix<var,Dynamic,Dynamic>
subtract(const Matrix<T1,Dynamic,Dynamic>& m,
const T2& c) {
Matrix<var,Dynamic,Dynamic> mc(m.rows(),m.cols());
for (int i = 0; i < c.size(); ++i)
mc(i) = m(i) - c;
return mc;
}

A single templated function could work for all four cases
of double/var for T1 and T2:

template <typename T1, typename T2>
inline Matrix<typename promote_args<T1,T2>::type,Dynamic,Dynamic>
subtract(const Matrix<T1,Dynamic,Dynamic>& m,
const T2& c) {
Matrix<typename promote_args<T1,T2>::type,Dynamic,Dynamic>
mc(m.rows(),m.cols());
for (int i = 0; i < c.size(); ++i)
mc(i) = m(i) - c;
return mc;
}

In fact, if you pull out the two Dynamic template params and replace
them with template params, you could generalize across vectors,
row vectors and matrices, too -- they all support size() and
unary operator() for references.

But as you saw, I've broken these down into separate functions
because all the auto-dif stuff needs a round of unfolding
for optimization (as we've done with the basic functions
you see in stan/agrad/agrad.hpp). And the doc's also a lot
easier than the mess of promotions above.

Also, I've been un-inlining anything that has loops like this.
In general, we only want to inline fairly short programs. Of
course, the compiler probably won't inline the big ones anyway -- it's
only a suggestion.

- Bob

?? for EVERYONE:
-----------------
As to this specific patch (and presumably its sibling,
addition by scalar), what does everyone else think about
having this kind of broadcasting of constants up to
appropriately sized vectors or matrices?  With v a vector,
m a matrix, and c a scalar, this would be:

 vector:  (v - c)(i) = v(i) - c

 matrix:  (m - c)(i,j) = m(i,j) - c

Is this something that's done in MATLAB?  In standard
vector notation?

This is MATLAB's convention and to me it is relatively unambiguous and allows for reasonable optimization.  The other ways to handle the functionality that I've seen include:

1) require users to define extra "transformed parameters" which manually build vectors and matrices full of the constant
2) provide a ones() function or something similar which produces a matrix (or vector) of appropriate size which can then be multiplied by the desired constant
3) interpret +/- constants as operating on each element of a matrix/vector (what I implemented)

(1) is cumbersome and potentially leads to excess memory usage, although it would be reasonably fast in terms of computation.  (2) is the slowest of the options, providing little ability to optimize the code as the intention of the user is hard to discern.  That said, functions like ones() and eye() (for identity matrices) are generally handy to have.  So I went with (3) since it allows for relatively efficient implementation if done properly (what I did probably isn't).

I also have some (long) comments on efficiency and some of
the standards we've tried to follow.  Your implementation (for
matrices) is:

   inline matrix_d subtract(const matrix_d& m, const double& c) {
     matrix_d c_(m.rows(),m.cols());
     c_.fill(c);
     return m - c_;
   }

I'm wondering if it'd be more efficient to do this explicitly:

   inline matrix_d subtract(const matrix_d& m, const double c) {
       matrix_d mc(m.rows(),m.cols());
       for (int i = 0; i < c.size(); ++i)
           mc(i) = m(i) - c;
       return mc;
   }

This unfortunately relies on fixed row-major or column-major
ordering because it uses unary accessors.

But then your last line, "return m - c_;" should be using
a template expression for (m - c_) rather than allocating, so
the return-by-value should copy directly without creating
an intermediate in situations like:

    matrix_d mc = m - c;

So they're probably very similar in terms of performance, with
the only difference being the second loop through the data
done by fill(c).

Assuming Eigen/the compiler is smart, I would think fill() for basic numeric types would reduce to a memset() call which is itself notably faster than looping and repeatedly indexing.  I could certainly be wrong.

?? for BEN:
-----------
What we'd really like is a no-allocation template expression
for a constant M x N matrix (like your "c_"), but I can't figure
out how to do that in Eigen (CwiseNullaryOp, as returned
by Constant() looks promising).  Ben?

Alternatively, Eigen directly supports adding/subtracting a scalar from each element of an Array type object.  Unfortunately, I wasn't able to figure out how to make this work.  If I understand Eigen's docs properly you can do it with matrices like so:

  return (m.array() - c).matrix();

but I'm not sure about the conversion back to vector types.

We've saved the "x_" style of variables for class member variables
to separate them visually from local variables (we've also been
inconsistent and used "_x" and I used "x__" inside of models to
avoid name clashes with Stan variables).
Ah, sorry, my bad.  I'll use that naming convention going forward.

I haven't profiled, but every piece of advice I've ever
seen says that doubles should be passed by value where
possible.  There are some clever ways to template out an arg
so that it's by value for primitives and otherwise by ref --
Alexandrescu discusses this in his C++ book and the approach
is implemented more or less in Boost.

In retrospect that's probably true for 64bit machines.  On 32bit machines I'd always been told that it's faster to pass by reference since it's half the amount data getting pushed onto the stack.  For inlined function it's largely irrelevant, so long as the function doesn't modify the value of the double.

But we haven't gone that
far down the optimization path, yet.  I'd rather get things
working before getting too carried away on optimization (despite
how I may sound in this e-mail).
Fair enough.  That said I've always found it worth thinking about throughout.  Design decisions made now can have performance impacts that could be hard or tedious to fix later.

We don't want to promote a matrix or vector of scalars to
an auto dif variable (using to_var()) unless we have to,
as the creation of auto-dif variables is expensive.
I plan to go back in and optimize all the vector ops to
avoid many of the to_var() that are there and also partially
evaluate the auto-difs as we've already done for the basic
functions.
I'll try to go back and rework what I've done in those terms.

But as you saw, I've broken these down into separate functions
because all the auto-dif stuff needs a round of unfolding
for optimization (as we've done with the basic functions
you see in stan/agrad/agrad.hpp).  And the doc's also a lot
easier than the mess of promotions above.
I'm not sure I follow you in terms of the docs.  Having dozens of "add" functions compared to one seems more confusing to me or am I missing your meaning?

Also, I've been un-inlining anything that has loops like this.
In general, we only want to inline fairly short programs.  Of
course, the compiler probably won't inline the big ones anyway -- it's
only a suggestion.

Yeah, I've generally understood inline to be more about allowing the compiler to inline it if it chooses to, rather than forcing it to do anything.  My only argument for keeping those inlined is that ideally most of those loops would eventually go away and be replaced by modular calls to other appropriate functions and at that point someone would need to remember to add the inline designation back in.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Patch adding matrix/vector scalar subtraction (plus bug fix)
parts:
Ok, take two.

I realized that the various vector types are just specialized Matrix templates (a retrospective duh) so I can use the .array()/.matrix() trick to implement the addition/subtraction of elements cleanly and efficiently.  I've also templated the functions to avoid code duplication, removed the pass-by-reference doubles and implemented addition.

By the way, is there a reason to differentiate the matrix/vector/row_vector functions instead of templating them?

I've attached a patch for now.  If I get commit access I can commit it assuming that it passes muster.

I think the .array()/.matrix() trick could be used to avoid the loops in the elementwise multiplication and division as well as I think those operators are defined there.  If you'd like I can go ahead and do that and send a patch.

Cheers,
Marcus

I finally bit the bullet and tracked down what was
going on in Eigen (I was more curious than concerned about
the case we're looking at).

Your intuitions are right, but for the wrong reason.

fill() is just an alias for setConstant, which does this
(from CwiseNullaryOp.h in Eigen/Core):

template<typename Derived>
EIGEN_STRONG_INLINE Derived&
PlainObjectBase<Derived>::setConstant(Index rows, Index cols, const
Scalar& value)
{
resize(rows, cols);
return setConstant(value);
}

which calls this:

template<typename Derived>
EIGEN_STRONG_INLINE Derived& DenseBase<Derived>::setConstant(const
Scalar& value)
{
return derived() = Constant(rows(), cols(), value);
}

The derived() thing is from their use of the so-called curiously
recurring template pattern. This then calls this method:

template<typename Derived>
EIGEN_STRONG_INLINE const typename DenseBase<Derived>::ConstantReturnType
DenseBase<Derived>::Constant(Index rows, Index cols, const Scalar& value)
{
return DenseBase<Derived>::NullaryExpr(rows, cols,
internal::scalar_constant_op<Scalar>(value));
}

which then calls:

template<typename Derived>
template<typename CustomNullaryOp>
EIGEN_STRONG_INLINE const CwiseNullaryOp<CustomNullaryOp, Derived>
DenseBase<Derived>::NullaryExpr(Index rows, Index cols, const
CustomNullaryOp& func)
{
return CwiseNullaryOp<CustomNullaryOp, Derived>(rows, cols, func);
}

and finally, we construct the CwiseNullaryOp, which only stores the
number of rows, number of columns, and the functor (which is just
a single value promoted in the second to last call above).

> We've saved the "x_" style of variables for class member variables

That's the general advice for both 32-bit and 64-bit situations.
It will probably depend on how the variable gets used in the function,
but the problem with refs is that you need to chase pointers, then
bring the 64 bits into registers. This is going to be
way more expensive than copying an extra 32 bits in terms
of memory non-locality, which is the main killer given how much
faster CPUs are than memory these days.

Even some structs, like our var, could probably be as efficiently,
if not more efficiently, passed by value. They're just pointers
to implementation, so they're only 8 bytes.

Again, this is something we can play with later.

But I doubt anyone's going to use the doxygen doc anyway.
It's almost useless for Boost and Eigen in my experience,
given their insane levels of complexity.

> Also, I've been un-inlining anything that has loops like this.

> course, the compiler probably won't inline the big ones anyway -- it's

>
>

Either way, we'll profile when we want to do the next

R has diag() and Diag().  diag() takes a vector as input and creates a diagonal matrix.  If you give diag a single scalar it creates a matrix, i.e, diag(5) is the same as diag(rep(1,5)).  Diag() takes a square matrix as input and outputs the vector of diagonals.

I'd rather use diag() than id() or eye().
